body: Gum trees (eucalyptus) are the most common tree in Australia, with light bark and puffy clusters of leaves. Their appearance can vary depending on location.
Australian bollards are white with a red reflector on the front and grey on the back; New Zealand’s bollard has a red reflector wrapping around the back.
Australia drives on the left. A few other countries also drive on the left.
Almost all road lines in Australia are white. If you see yellow lines, you might be in South Africa or New Zealand instead.
Rumble strips appear as small white stripes on outside lines in Australia. They are rare in the Northern Territory, and similar strips are found in New Zealand.
Give-way signs in Australia have a white border and black text. In New Zealand, these signs use red text.
Australia uses white on black and black on yellow chevrons.
Green signs with white arrows show nearby towns or cities and may include a kilometre number.
Australian speed limit signs display black text in a red circle on a large white rectangle, unlike New Zealand's which typically lack this background.
A long antenna is visible on Generation 3 coverage cars in Australia.
Each Australian state has distinct licence plate designs, sometimes visible despite blurring.
Australian phone numbers have 8 digits plus a 2-digit area code, but not all numbers show the area code.
Every state has a unique bus stop design; Darwin uses concrete shelters, Tasmanian stops usually say 'metro'.
Stobie poles made of steel and concrete are unique to South Australia. Pole tops also have distinctive shapes.
Rusty metal poles with holes are unique to the Northern Territory, but may be found in parts of northern WA.
Around 64% of concrete poles in Australia are located in Victoria.
Trident-like pole tops can be found in Western Australia and Victoria.
Queensland pole tops have upward angled coils on the sides.
Victorian pole tops have three coils; two on the sides and one vertical at the top, sometimes with other extensions.
Tasmanian pole tops often have a thin metal L-shaped crossbar; typical Australian crossbars are wood.
Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles; similar stickers, sometimes faded or different colors, may occur elsewhere.
Black markings are specific to Queensland electricity poles, often accompanied by diagonal numbers.
Olive-green possum guards are only found on Tasmanian electricity poles; the color is the main identifier.
Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, sometimes with a white sticker or a red and white band.
Short reflectors are most common in Queensland and South Australia, but appear in every state.
Bollards with brown paint at the base are mainly found in Western Australia; other states rarely have them and the brown section is smaller.
Black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.
The black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.
Yellow signposts are characteristic of Western Australia; SA bus stops use yellow posts but not for regular signs.
Signposts in South Australia and Western Australia may be flat instead of round, often yellow in WA.
Signposts in the Northern Territory sometimes have yellow stickers.
Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost only found in Queensland.
New South Wales alone uses red 'No Stopping' signs; other states use white versions.
White 'No Stopping' and 'No Parking' signs with text are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.
White directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.
Roads starting with 'C' are only found in Victoria and Tasmania, with some near the SA border.
A 25 speed limit in school zones is specific to South Australia.
Australia’s 130 km/h speed limit exists only in the Northern Territory.
Some 'Keep Left' signs in NSW, QLD, and NT have a thinner look without an arrow.
Traffic lights with a white outline on the frame are seen in WA, QLD, NSW, ACT, and Tas; central states use lights without a border.
Dark green property markers are found on roadsides in Western Australia.
White property markers are found on roadsides in South Australia.
Guardrail endings with a black dash on yellow are almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.
White hydrant poles with a blue circle and a red section on top are found in Victoria.
Fire hydrants with red painted tops are unique to Victoria.
Western Australia, especially Perth, is known for its reddish-orange soil, but light soil also appears in parts of WA and other states.
Brush plants are common in Western Australia.
Darwin is famous for dark red soil, rich green grass, and trees with black trunks.
Termite mounds sometimes appear in the Northern Territory and rarely in northern WA and QLD as brown, spiky ground formations.
The dry area from SA to WA has shrubs, wide crowned eucalyptus, and sandy, orange-tinted soil; it gets drier east of Adelaide and whiter into NW Victoria.
Lush fields span from the south Yorke Peninsula to Echuca, with drier land on the SA side and taller, leafier trees in Victoria.
Coastal northern Queensland is tropical with palms and dark green vegetation.
Sugarcane plantations are common in northern Queensland’s tropical regions but can be seen as far south as northern NSW.
Inland NSW landscapes are flat with redder soil and dry pale-green shrubs, transitioning to sandier soil and more eucalyptus toward the east and borders.
Tasmania has a cool temperate climate, green rolling hills, and dense eucalyptus forests, with landscapes similar to Chile or New Zealand.
Generation 2 coverage is not found in the Northern Territory.
Australia has rare Google cars with snorkels mostly in NSW and ACT, designed for flooded terrain; a few are in WA.
Christmas Island and Cocos (Keeling) Islands are counted as part of Australia with unique cars easy to identify.
Tom Price area has red soil, Generation 2 camera, and rocky hills.
Alice Springs is marked by distinct orange rocks visible in the distance or at road ends.
Cairns stands out for its tropical vegetation, large green mountains, and many urban high-rise buildings.
Mount Gambier features white soil and extensive pine tree plantations.
Kangaroo Island in SA has bushy vegetation, stubby eucalyptus, orange soil and only Generation 2/4 coverage.
The Nullarbor Highway is very flat with grey colors and sparse vegetation.
A wire on the left is seen along much of the Barkly Highway in the NT and part of QLD.
Dorat Road 23 in the Northern Territory stands out due to its Darwin-area landscape and lack of road lines.
The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga may have triple broken centre lines, also seen on other major NSW roads.
The Stuart Highway (Alice Springs to Pimba, SA) stands out for bright orange dirt, short trees, and Generation 4 blue cars.
In Perth, some kerbs are sloped to the road, unlike the usual sharp 90-degree drop in other cities.
Melbourne poles often show white rectangular stickers with a smaller blue square inside.
All-yellow road lines are seen near Mount Kosciuszko and in other alpine locations; look for white trucks with snorkels and cab guards.
South Australian style Stobie poles can be sometimes found in Broken Hill, NSW.
This street sign is unique to Brisbane City Council.
This street sign is unique to Gold Coast City Council.
This street sign is unique to the City of Sydney.
